---
title: "A3 exercises — Exchange, blood and flow"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Diffusion and exchange surfaces

### 1.1

For each step in the path of oxygen from air to a mammalian muscle
mitochondrion, state whether the main process is bulk flow or diffusion.

a. air moving through the trachea and bronchi to the alveoli
b. O₂ crossing the alveolar wall and capillary endothelium into the plasma
c. blood carrying O₂ from the lungs to the muscle
d. O₂ moving from the muscle capillary to the mitochondria

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Bulk flow (ventilation). b. Diffusion. c. Bulk flow (circulation).
d. Diffusion.
:::

### 1.2

Dry air at sea level has a total pressure of 101.3 kPa and contains 20.9 %
O₂. Calculate the partial pressure of O₂.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

$P_{\rm O_2}=0.209\times101.3\ \text{kPa}=21.2$ kPa (about 159 mmHg).
:::

### 1.3

Use Fick's relationship $\dot M\propto A\,\Delta P/L$, with the diffusion
properties of the barrier held constant. Surface 1 has area 10 units,
thickness 2 units and partial-pressure difference 4 units. Surface 2 has twice
the area, twice the thickness and half the partial-pressure difference.
Calculate the transfer rate across surface 2 relative to surface 1.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Surface 1: $10\times4/2=20$. Surface 2: $20\times2/4=10$. Transfer across
surface 2 is half that across surface 1 ($2\times\tfrac12/2=0.5$).
:::

### 1.4

Define *ventilation* and *perfusion*, and state how each helps to maintain the
partial-pressure gradient across a respiratory surface.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Ventilation:** bulk flow of the respiratory medium (air or water) over the
  respiratory surface. It replaces medium from which O₂ has been taken, keeping
  external $P_{\rm O_2}$ high.
- **Perfusion:** bulk flow of blood (or other internal fluid) through the
  respiratory surface. It removes O₂-loaded blood and brings O₂-poor blood,
  keeping internal $P_{\rm O_2}$ low.
:::

## Gills, lungs and tracheae

### 2.1

Name the main gas-exchange structure in each animal.

a. bony fish
b. mammal
c. bird
d. insect

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Gill lamellae (secondary lamellae of the gill filaments). b. Alveoli of the
lungs. c. Air capillaries of the parabronchi in the lungs. d. Tracheoles, the
fine endings of the tracheal system.
:::

### 2.2

The values below are O₂ partial pressures (kPa) along a fish gill lamella.
Water flows from position 1 to position 4; blood flows from position 4 to
position 1.

| Position | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Water $P_{\rm O_2}$ | 20 | 16 | 12 | 8 |
| Blood $P_{\rm O_2}$ | 18 | 14 | 10 | 6 |

a. Give the $P_{\rm O_2}$ of the water entering and leaving, and of the blood
   entering and leaving the lamella.
b. In which direction does O₂ diffuse at each position, and what is the local
   partial-pressure difference?
c. What is this flow arrangement called?
d. If blood and water flowed in the same direction, could the blood leave with
   a higher $P_{\rm O_2}$ than the water leaving? Explain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Water enters at 20 kPa and leaves at 8 kPa. Blood enters at 6 kPa and
   leaves at 18 kPa.
b. From water to blood at every position; the difference is 2 kPa everywhere.
c. Countercurrent exchange.
d. No. In co-current flow the two streams approach the same $P_{\rm O_2}$, so
   blood can at most equal the $P_{\rm O_2}$ of the water leaving. In
   countercurrent flow, blood leaves at 18 kPa, higher than the water leaving
   (8 kPa), although O₂ always diffuses down the local gradient.
:::

### 2.3

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. In mammals, air flows in one direction through the lungs.
b. In birds, the air sacs are the main gas-exchange surface.
c. In insects, the haemolymph carries most of the O₂ to the tissues.
d. Part of each breath in a mammal stays in the conducting airways and does
   not reach the alveoli.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. Mammalian ventilation is tidal: air moves in and out through the same
   airways.
b. False. Exchange occurs in the parabronchi of the rigid lungs; the air sacs
   act as bellows that ventilate the lungs, giving one-way flow through the
   parabronchi.
c. False. The tracheal system carries O₂ in gas phase directly to the tissues;
   haemolymph has a small role in O₂ transport.
d. True. This volume is the anatomical dead space.
:::

## Oxygen and carbon dioxide in blood

### 3.1

Define *partial pressure of O₂*, *haemoglobin saturation* and *O₂ content*
of blood, and give a unit for each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **$P_{\rm O_2}$:** the pressure exerted by O₂ (in blood, by the dissolved,
  unbound O₂); kPa or mmHg.
- **Saturation:** the percentage of haemoglobin O₂-binding sites that are
  occupied; %.
- **O₂ content:** the total amount of O₂ (bound plus dissolved) per volume of
  blood; mL O₂ L⁻¹.
:::

### 3.2

Each gram of haemoglobin binds at most 1.34 mL O₂. Blood contains 150 g
haemoglobin per litre. Ignore dissolved O₂.

a. Calculate the O₂ content at 100 % saturation.
b. Calculate the O₂ content at 75 % saturation.
c. An anaemic person has 75 g haemoglobin per litre and the same arterial
   $P_{\rm O_2}$ and saturation (98 %) as a healthy person. Calculate their
   arterial O₂ content and state which of $P_{\rm O_2}$, saturation and
   content differ from the healthy person.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. $150\times1.34=201$ mL O₂ L⁻¹.
b. $0.75\times201=151$ mL O₂ L⁻¹.
c. $75\times1.34\times0.98=98$ mL O₂ L⁻¹. Only the content differs (it is
   halved); $P_{\rm O_2}$ and saturation are unchanged.
:::

### 3.3

Why is the haemoglobin–O₂ dissociation curve sigmoid (S-shaped)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Haemoglobin has four subunits that bind O₂ cooperatively: binding of O₂ to one
subunit increases the O₂ affinity of the others. Affinity is therefore low at
low $P_{\rm O_2}$ and high at intermediate $P_{\rm O_2}$, giving a steep middle
part to the curve.
:::

### 3.4

State whether each change shifts the haemoglobin–O₂ dissociation curve to the
right or to the left, and whether it favours O₂ unloading in the tissues.

a. increased $P_{\rm CO_2}$
b. decreased pH
c. decreased temperature
d. increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in red blood cells

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Right; favours unloading. b. Right; favours unloading (Bohr effect).
c. Left; reduces unloading. d. Right; favours unloading.

A right shift means lower affinity: less O₂ is bound at a given $P_{\rm O_2}$.
:::

### 3.5

a. Name the three forms in which CO₂ is carried in mammalian blood, from the
   largest to the smallest fraction.
b. Write the reaction catalysed by carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells,
   including the dissociation of the product.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Bicarbonate ions (about 70 %), bound to haemoglobin as carbamino compounds
   (about 20 %), dissolved CO₂ (about 10 %).
b. $\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-}$.
   Carbonic anhydrase catalyses the first step.
:::

## Circulation

### 4.1

Put the structures in order, starting from the systemic veins, for blood
flowing through a mammal: left atrium, pulmonary veins, right ventricle,
systemic arteries, lung capillaries, left ventricle, right atrium, pulmonary
arteries.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Systemic veins → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lung
capillaries → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → systemic
arteries.
:::

### 4.2

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Arteries always carry oxygenated blood.
b. Heart valves prevent the backflow of blood.
c. In a fish, blood passes through the heart once for each complete circuit
   of the body.
d. In an open circulatory system, the circulating fluid does not move.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The pulmonary arteries
   carry deoxygenated blood.
b. True.
c. True. Fish have a single circulation: heart → gills → systemic tissues →
   heart.
d. False. Haemolymph is pumped by the heart and flows through vessels and
   body spaces (sinuses) before returning to the heart.
:::

### 4.3

Classify the circulatory system of each animal as open or closed.

a. earthworm
b. grasshopper
c. octopus
d. mussel
e. frog

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Closed. b. Open. c. Closed. d. Open. e. Closed.
:::

### 4.4

Complete the table.

| | Artery | Capillary | Vein |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direction of flow relative to the heart | | | |
| Wall | | | |
| Blood pressure | | | |
| Main function | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Artery | Capillary | Vein |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direction of flow relative to the heart | Away from the heart | Between arterioles and venules | Towards the heart |
| Wall | Thick, with much elastic tissue and smooth muscle | Endothelium only, one cell thick | Thin, with little smooth muscle; valves in many limb veins |
| Blood pressure | High, pulsatile | Low | Lowest |
| Main function | Carry blood under pressure to the tissues | Exchange with the tissues | Return blood to the heart; hold most of the blood volume |
:::

### 4.5

Use $Q=\Delta P/R$.

a. The pressure difference across a vascular bed stays constant while its
   resistance doubles. By what factor does flow change?
b. Resistance of a tube is proportional to $1/r^4$, where $r$ is the radius.
   By what factor does resistance change when an arteriole constricts to half
   its radius?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Flow halves.
b. $2^4=16$: resistance increases sixteen-fold, so at constant $\Delta P$
   flow falls to 1/16.
:::

### 4.6

At rest, heart rate is 80 beats min⁻¹, stroke volume 0.050 L beat⁻¹,
arterial O₂ content 190 mL O₂ L⁻¹ and mixed venous O₂ content 140 mL O₂ L⁻¹.
During exercise, heart rate is 120 beats min⁻¹, stroke volume 0.080 L beat⁻¹
and the arterial–venous O₂ content difference 100 mL O₂ L⁻¹.

a. Calculate cardiac output at rest and during exercise.
b. Calculate whole-body O₂ consumption at rest and during exercise (Fick
   principle).
c. By what factor does O₂ consumption increase?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Rest: $80\times0.050=4.0$ L min⁻¹. Exercise: $120\times0.080=9.6$ L min⁻¹.
b. Rest: $4.0\times(190-140)=200$ mL O₂ min⁻¹. Exercise:
   $9.6\times100=960$ mL O₂ min⁻¹.
c. $960/200=4.8$. Both cardiac output and the O₂ extraction from each litre of
   blood increased.
:::

## Explore: Haemoglobin loading and unloading {#explore-a3-dissociation}

The blue curve is haemoglobin under lung conditions, where blood loads at the
arterial PO₂; the red curve is the same haemoglobin under the tissue's pH and
temperature, where it unloads at the tissue PO₂. Use the sliders or presets, or
drag the red point; read the results from the readout below the sliders.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a3-dissociation"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a3-dissociation.js"></script>
```

### E1

Press **Rest**. Read off (a) the tissue P₅₀, (b) the percentage of
haemoglobin that is unloaded (gold bar) and (c) the O₂ delivered per litre of
blood. Compare (c) with the arterial–venous O₂ difference at rest in
question 4.6.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 3.6 kPa (tissue pH 7.37 shifts the curve very slightly right of 3.5 kPa).
b. 24 % (arterial 97 %, venous 74 %).
c. 48 mL O₂ L⁻¹ (196 − 148). This is close to the 50 mL O₂ L⁻¹ a–v difference
   in question 4.6: at rest only about a quarter of the O₂ is used.
:::

### E2

Press **Exercise, no shift** and read the O₂ delivered per litre. Then press
**Exercise** and read it again. Starting from the rest value in E1, which
contributes more to the extra O₂ delivered during exercise?

a. the fall in tissue PO₂ from 5.3 to 2.7 kPa
b. the right shift of the curve (pH 7.2, 39 °C)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Exercise, no shift: 129 mL O₂ L⁻¹. Exercise: 162 mL O₂ L⁻¹.

a. The fall in tissue PO₂ adds 129 − 48 = 81 mL O₂ L⁻¹; the right shift adds a
further 162 − 129 = 33 mL O₂ L⁻¹. The low PO₂ lies on the steep part of the
curve, where a small drop in PO₂ releases a lot of O₂.
:::

### E3

Press **Exercise**. Set **Tissue temp.** back to 37 °C (pH stays at 7.2) and
read the O₂ delivered. Then press **Exercise** again and set **Tissue pH** back
to 7.40 (temperature stays at 39 °C) and read it again. Which part of the
exercise right shift, acidity (Bohr effect) or warming, contributes more in this
model?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

pH 7.2 at 37 °C: 153 mL O₂ L⁻¹ (P₅₀ 4.4 kPa). pH 7.4 at 39 °C: 142 mL O₂ L⁻¹
(P₅₀ 3.9 kPa). Acidity contributes more: it alone gives most of the
33 mL O₂ L⁻¹ gain of the full exercise shift.
:::

### E4

Press **Altitude** (arterial PO₂ 6.5 kPa, about half the sea-level value). Read
off the arterial saturation and arterial O₂ content, and compare them with the
**Rest** values (97 %, 196 mL O₂ L⁻¹). Which statement is correct?

a. Saturation falls in proportion to PO₂, to about half.
b. Saturation falls much less than PO₂, because sea-level loading takes place on
   the flat top of the curve.
c. Saturation does not change, because the curve is flat everywhere above
   5 kPa.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Arterial saturation 84 %, content 169 mL O₂ L⁻¹. b: halving PO₂ lowers
saturation by only 13 percentage points, because the arterial point moves from
the plateau down onto the shoulder of the sigmoid curve.
:::

### E5

Press **Anaemia** ([Hb] 100 instead of 150 g L⁻¹) and compare with **Rest**.
Which of the readouts change? Give the O₂ delivered per litre.

a. the percentage unloaded only
b. the O₂ contents and the O₂ delivered only
c. both

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b. The saturations (97 % and 74 %) and the 24 % unloaded are the same as at
rest, because the curve depends on PO₂, pH and temperature, not on how much
haemoglobin there is. The O₂ delivered falls from 48 to 32 mL O₂ L⁻¹, by one
third, in proportion to [Hb] (capacity 1.34 mL O₂ per g Hb).
:::

## Explore: Countercurrent exchange in the gill {#explore-a3-countercurrent}

A model gill lamella: water enters at 20 kPa from the left, blood enters at
2 kPa, from the right (countercurrent) or from the left (co-current). Switch the
arrangement with the buttons and change the exchanger size and the blood-to-water
flow ratio with the sliders; the readout gives the outflowing PO₂ values and the
share of O₂ taken from the water.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a3-countercurrent"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a3-countercurrent.js"></script>
```

### E6

Press **Reset** (countercurrent, exchanger size 5, blood ÷ water flow 1.00).
Read off the PO₂ of the blood and the water leaving the lamella, the mean
water–blood gradient and the O₂ taken from the water. Then press **Co-current**
and read the same four values.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Blood out | Water out | Mean gradient | O₂ taken |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Countercurrent | 17.0 kPa | 5.0 kPa | 3.0 kPa | 75 % |
| Co-current | 11.0 kPa | 11.0 kPa | 1.9 kPa | 45 % |

In co-current flow the two streams approach the same PO₂ and the exchange
stops; in countercurrent flow a gradient is kept along the whole lamella.
:::

### E7

Set the exchanger size to 10 (flow ratio 1.00) and read the blood PO₂ out in
each arrangement. In which arrangement can the blood leave with a higher PO₂
than the water leaving the gill?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Countercurrent: 18.4 kPa (water leaves at 3.6 kPa). Co-current: 11.0 kPa, the
same as at size 5. Only countercurrent: in co-current flow the blood can at best
equilibrate with the outflowing water, the mixed value of 11 kPa, however large
the exchanger.
:::

### E8

In countercurrent mode with exchanger size 5, set **Blood ÷ water flow** to
0.50 and then to 2.00. For each, read the blood PO₂ out and the O₂ taken from
the water. Which statement is correct?

a. Low blood flow gives the highest blood PO₂ but extracts less of the O₂ in the
   water.
b. High blood flow gives both the highest blood PO₂ and the highest extraction.
c. The flow ratio does not matter in countercurrent exchange.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Ratio 0.50: blood out 19.9 kPa, 45 % taken. Ratio 2.00: blood out 10.6 kPa,
86 % taken. a: slow blood almost reaches the inlet water's PO₂, while fast
blood strips more O₂ from the water but leaves less saturated. Fish adjust
ventilation and lamellar perfusion to match the two.
:::

## Bioinformatics and R {#bioinformatics}

The bar-headed goose (*Anser indicus*) breeds on lakes in Tibet and migrates
over the Himalaya to winter in India. Its close relative, the greylag goose
(*Anser anser*), lives at low altitude. In blood taken under standard
conditions, the haemoglobin of the bar-headed goose binds O₂ with higher
affinity. The exercises below track down the molecular cause and test whether
it matters. The new skills in this unit are **BLAST** (finding related
sequences and reading E-value and % identity), telling **orthologs from
paralogs**, and **multiple sequence alignment with Clustal Omega**. R is used
to read the sequences straight from UniProt, find the differences, and model
O₂ saturation at altitude with the **Hill equation**. Only base R is used; run
the code in R or RStudio with an internet connection.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to use BLAST and Clustal Omega

**BLAST** (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) compares one query sequence with
every sequence in a database and lists the most similar ones. Go to
<https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov>, choose **Protein BLAST** (blastp: protein
query against protein database) and paste a sequence or a UniProt accession
(for example `P01990`) into the query box. Under *Database*, choose
**UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (swissprot)**, the reviewed proteins you met in A1.
Optionally type a species in *Organism* (for example `Homo sapiens
(taxid:9606)`) to search only that species. Under *Algorithm parameters*,
*Max target sequences* sets how many hits are listed. Press **BLAST** and wait
up to a minute.

In the results table, each row is one hit:

- **Per. ident** (% identity): the percentage of aligned positions with the
  same amino acid. Click a hit to see the alignment and the exact
  "Identities" fraction, for example 139/142.
- **E value**: how many hits this good you would expect by pure chance in a
  database of this size. Values far below 1 (such as 1e-50) mean the
  similarity is not chance, so the proteins share an ancestor (they are
  **homologous**). Values near 1 or above mean nothing. E-values change a
  little when the database grows, so read only their order of magnitude.

Homologous genes come in two kinds. **Orthologs** are the same gene in
different species; they separated when the species split (goose and human
haemoglobin α). **Paralogs** arose by a gene duplication within one genome
and then took on different jobs (human haemoglobin α, haemoglobin β and
myoglobin).

**Clustal Omega** aligns three or more sequences so that corresponding
residues sit in the same column. Go to
<https://www.ebi.ac.uk/jdispatcher/msa/clustalo>, set the sequence type to
*Protein*, paste the sequences in FASTA format (each one starting with a `>`
line, as downloaded from UniProt) and submit. In the alignment, `*` under a
column means the residue is identical in all sequences, `:` similar and `.`
weakly similar. The **Results Summary** tab has a **Percent Identity Matrix**
with the identity of every pair.
:::

### B1. Who are the goose's closest relatives?

Run a protein BLAST with the bar-headed goose haemoglobin α-A chain, UniProt
**P01990**, against UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot. Set *Max target sequences* to 1000.

a. The first hit is the query itself (100 %). Which species gives the next
   hit, and what is its accession?
b. Open the alignment of that hit. What is the "Identities" fraction, and how
   many amino acids differ between the two α chains?
c. The E-value of this hit is far below 1 (about 1e-99). What does that tell
   you?
   (i) The two proteins are unrelated.
   (ii) A match this good would essentially never arise by chance, so the
   proteins are homologous.
   (iii) The two proteins have identical functions.
d. The first hundred or so hits are α chains of other birds. Scroll further
   down (or use the browser's find function) to human haemoglobin subunit α,
   P69905. Roughly what is its % identity to the goose chain: about 50 %,
   70 % or 90 %?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. The western greylag goose, *Anser anser anser*: P01989 (HBA_ANSAN). Further
   down come Canada goose, Muscovy duck, wigeon, mallard and other waterfowl.
b. 139/142 (about 98 % identity): only 3 amino acids differ. These three
   differences are the candidates for the higher O₂ affinity.
c. (ii). A low E-value shows common ancestry. It does not prove the same
   function; that has to be tested (B5).
d. About 70 % (69 %, 98 of 142 residues). Bird α chains are about 85–98 %
   identical to the goose chain, mammal α chains about 70 %: identity falls
   with the time since the species shared an ancestor.
:::

### B2. Orthologs or paralogs?

Run the same BLAST again, but type `Homo sapiens (taxid:9606)` in
*Organism*. All hits are now human globins.

a. Which human protein is the top hit, and what is its % identity (to the
   nearest whole percent)?
b. Find haemoglobin subunit β (HBB) and myoglobin (MB) in the human list.
   Order the three human proteins α, β and myoglobin from most to least
   similar to the goose α-A chain.
c. Classify each pair as orthologs or paralogs:
   (1) goose α-A (P01990) and human α (P69905),
   (2) human α (P69905) and human β (P68871),
   (3) human β and human myoglobin (P02144).
d. Download the FASTA of P01990, P69905, P68871 and P02144 from UniProt and
   align them in Clustal Omega. In the Percent Identity Matrix, which pair of
   *human* proteins is the most similar: α–β, α–myoglobin or β–myoglobin?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Haemoglobin subunit α (P69905, gene *HBA1*/*HBA2*), about 69 % identical
   (98/142).
b. α (about 69 %) > β (about 35 %) > myoglobin (about 25 %, with an E-value of
   only about 1e-7). Further human hits include the embryonic ζ chain and the
   fetal γ chains.
c. (1) orthologs: the same gene in two species. (2) paralogs: α and β come
   from an ancient gene duplication and now form the α₂β₂ tetramer together.
   (3) paralogs: myoglobin split off even earlier and stays a single-chain O₂
   store in muscle.
d. α–β (about 39 %); both are ≈ 25 % identical to myoglobin. Paralogs that
   split long ago can be less similar than orthologs from a bird and a mammal,
   which split about 300 million years ago.
:::

### B3. Find the high-altitude substitution

R can fetch both α chains from UniProt and list the positions where they
differ. The same is done for the β chains.

```r
get_seq <- function(acc) {
  fa <- readLines(paste0("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/", acc, ".fasta"))
  strsplit(paste(fa[-1], collapse = ""), "")[[1]]
}
diff_table <- function(x, y, names) {
  d <- which(x != y)
  setNames(data.frame(d, x[d], y[d]), c("position", names))
}
# alpha-A chains: bar-headed goose vs greylag goose
bar_a  <- get_seq("P01990")
grey_a <- get_seq("P01989")
length(bar_a); length(grey_a)
diff_table(bar_a, grey_a, c("bar_headed", "greylag"))
# beta chains
bar_b  <- get_seq("P02118")
grey_b <- get_seq("P02117")
diff_table(bar_b, grey_b, c("bar_headed", "greylag"))
```

a. List the α-chain differences as *greylag residue → bar-headed residue* at
   each UniProt position.
b. How many amino acids differ in total between the two haemoglobins (α plus
   β)?
c. UniProt counts the initial methionine as residue 1, but it is removed from
   the mature α chain, so haemoglobin researchers number from the next
   residue. In that classical numbering, where is the proline → alanine change?
d. Align P01990, P01989, P69905 (human α) and P07034 (Andean goose α) in
   Clustal Omega and find the column with the bar-headed alanine. Which residue
   do the other three sequences have there?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] 142
[1] 142
  position bar_headed greylag
1       19          S       G
2       64          V       A
3      120          A       P
  position bar_headed greylag
1      125          D       E
```

a. G19S, A64V and P120A (UniProt numbering).
b. Four: three in α and one in β.
c. α119 (Pro119α → Ala). Jessen et al. (1991, *PNAS* 88:6519) found that
   among the four differences only this one is unique among bird
   haemoglobins. Following a proposal by Max Perutz, they put the same change
   into human haemoglobin, and it raised the O₂ affinity.
d. Proline in all three. The proline is conserved from geese to humans, which
   suggests it is important. At α119 it touches the β chain (the α₁β₁
   contact). Alanine has a smaller side chain and leaves a gap there, which
   loosens the low-affinity (T) state, so O₂ binds more easily.
:::

### B4. The Andean goose found another way

The Andean goose (*Chloephaga melanoptera*) lives all year round in the high
Andes, on another continent. Does its haemoglobin carry the same change?
Run the code, which compares the β chains of the greylag and the Andean goose.
(The goose β chains in UniProt start without methionine, so here UniProt and
classical numbering agree; human β in UniProt includes the methionine.)

```r
get_seq <- function(acc) {
  fa <- readLines(paste0("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/", acc, ".fasta"))
  strsplit(paste(fa[-1], collapse = ""), "")[[1]]
}
grey_b   <- get_seq("P02117")   # greylag goose, lowland
andean_b <- get_seq("P07036")   # Andean goose, high altitude
human_b  <- get_seq("P68871")   # human
length(grey_b); length(andean_b); length(human_b)
d <- which(grey_b != andean_b)
data.frame(position = d, greylag = grey_b[d], andean = andean_b[d])
human_b[56]
```

a. Does the Andean goose α chain have the alanine at α119 (look at your
   alignment in B3d)?
b. How many positions differ between the greylag and Andean β chains?
c. Jessen et al. (1991) proposed one of these as the high-altitude change, a
   residue that contacts α119 across the α₁β₁ interface. It is a
   leucine → serine change. At which β position?
d. Which residue does human β have at the same position (classical β55,
   which is `human_b[56]` because of the methionine)?
e. Which statement fits B3 and B4?
   (i) Both geese inherited the same mutation from a common high-altitude
   ancestor.
   (ii) The two species evolved high O₂ affinity independently, by changes in
   different chains that open a gap at the same α₁β₁ contact.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] 146
[1] 146
[1] 147
  position greylag andean
1        4       S      T
2       43       S      A
3       55       L      S
4       86       A      S
5      119       A      T
6      121       E      D
7      125       E      D
[1] "M"
```

a. No, it has proline, like the greylag goose and human.
b. Seven.
c. β55 (Leu55β → Ser).
d. Methionine. Jessen et al. made the Met55β → Ser change in human haemoglobin,
   and it too raised O₂ affinity.
e. (ii). This is **convergent evolution** at the molecular level: two different
   substitutions, in α in one species and in β in the other, both remove bulk
   from the same contact between the subunits.
:::

### B5. Does it help at 9,000 m?

Petschow et al. (1977, *J. Appl. Physiol.* 42:139) measured whole-blood P₅₀ at
pH 7.4, PCO₂ 40 Torr and 37 °C: 29.7 Torr in the bar-headed goose and about
10 Torr higher (about 40 Torr) in lowland goose species. The code converts
these to kPa (1 Torr = 0.1333 kPa) and uses the Hill equation from this unit
with an assumed Hill coefficient of 2.5. It computes the inspired PO₂ from the
standard-atmosphere formula for barometric pressure, after subtracting water
vapour at bird body temperature (about 7.8 kPa) because inspired air is
saturated with water in the airways.

```r
# Whole-blood P50 at pH 7.4, 37 °C (Petschow et al. 1977), converted to kPa
p50 <- c(bar_headed = 29.7, lowland = 40) * 0.1333
round(p50, 1)
hill <- function(po2, p50, n = 2.5) po2^n / (po2^n + p50^n)   # n = 2.5 assumed

# Inspired PO2 at altitude h (m): standard-atmosphere pressure,
# minus water vapour at bird body temperature (7.8 kPa), times 20.95 % O2
pio2 <- function(h) 0.2095 * (101.325 * (1 - 2.25577e-5 * h)^5.25588 - 7.8)
h <- c(0, 3000, 6000, 9000)
round(pio2(h), 1)

round(100 * hill(pio2(0),    p50))   # sea level
round(100 * hill(pio2(9000), p50))   # over the Himalaya

# Altitude at which inspired PO2 has fallen to each P50
ceiling50 <- function(p) uniroot(function(h) pio2(h) - p, c(0, 15000))$root
round(sapply(p50, ceiling50), -2)

curve(100 * hill(x, p50["bar_headed"]), 0, 20, col = "blue",
      xlab = "PO2 (kPa)", ylab = "Haemoglobin saturation (%)")
curve(100 * hill(x, p50["lowland"]), add = TRUE, col = "red")
abline(v = pio2(c(0, 9000)), lty = 2)
```

a. What is the inspired PO₂ at sea level and at 9,000 m (about the height of
   the highest Himalayan peaks)?
b. If blood leaving the lungs reached the inspired PO₂ (a best case), what
   saturation would each goose reach at sea level, and at 9,000 m?
c. Up to which altitude (to the nearest 100 m) would the inspired PO₂ still be
   above P₅₀ for each goose?
d. In the plot, where do the two curves differ most?
   (i) at the right, near sea-level PO₂
   (ii) in the steep middle part, where PO₂ at high altitude lies
e. Real arterial PO₂ is lower than inspired PO₂. Does that make the advantage
   of the bar-headed goose haemoglobin smaller or larger, in percentage points
   of saturation?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
bar_headed    lowland
       4.0        5.3
[1] 19.6 13.1  8.3  4.8
bar_headed    lowland
        98         96
bar_headed    lowland
        62         44
bar_headed    lowland
      9900       8500
```

a. 19.6 kPa at sea level; 4.8 kPa at 9,000 m.
b. Sea level: 98 % and 96 %, almost no difference. At 9,000 m: 62 % against
   44 %, so the bar-headed goose carries about 40 % more O₂ per litre of blood
   from the same air.
c. About 9,900 m for the bar-headed goose and 8,500 m for the lowland goose.
d. (ii). On the flat top of the curve a higher affinity changes almost
   nothing; on the steep part, where PO₂ lies at high altitude, it changes
   saturation a lot.
e. Larger. Lower PO₂ moves both geese further down the steep part, where the
   gap between the curves is widest (compare the Explore demo: shifts of
   the curve matter most at mid-range PO₂). The cost is
   that a high-affinity haemoglobin releases O₂ less readily in the tissues,
   which is why it pays off only where O₂ is scarce.
:::
